one_liner: Broad C++ crypto class library; a 2013 hobby benchmark had its CAST-128-CBC about 1.3-1.4x faster than libgcrypt.
what_it_does: Crypto++ is a large C++ class library covering AEAD modes (GCM, CCM, EAX, ChaCha20-Poly1305, XChaCha20-Poly1305), dozens of block and stream ciphers, hashes, MACs, KDFs, public-key schemes and utilities such as DEFLATE and Base64. You either call the cipher objects directly (SetKeyWithIV, ProcessData, EncryptAndAuthenticate/DecryptAndVerify) or chain Source, Filter and Sink objects into a pipeline (StringSource to StreamTransformationFilter to StringSink). It is not a drop-in for libgcrypt or OpenSSL. The API, error model (C++ exceptions) and object ownership rules all differ.
how_it_is_fast: The CAST-128 code behind the measured numbers is a plain table-driven implementation: four 256-entry S-box lookups per round, one 8-byte block at a time, and 12 rounds for keys of 80 bits or less (cast.cpp). The 2013 margin over libgcrypt therefore reflects both libraries' code and call overhead at that time, not a special technique. CAST-128 also gets no multi-block SIMD path, because adv_simd.h says the library stopped using the 64-bit-block AdvancedProcessBlocks templates in July 2020. Elsewhere, Crypto++'s speed comes from ISA-specific translation units (AES-NI with SSE4.1, CLMUL with SSSE3 for GCM, AVX2 for ChaCha, SHA-NI, ARMv8 crypto/PMULL, POWER8) that are selected by runtime CPU detection. AdvancedProcessBlocks templates process 4 or 6 128-bit blocks at once for parallelisable modes such as CTR and CBC decryption, and GCM falls back to 2K or 64K GHASH tables without CLMUL.
when_to_use: An existing C++ codebase that needs one permissively licensed library (BSL-1.0 compilation, public-domain files) with an unusually wide algorithm set, including legacy ciphers (CAST-128, Blowfish, IDEA, Camellia, ARIA, SEED, SM4) for reading old formats or talking to old peers.

Old or unusual toolchains and targets. The 8.9 Readme lists support from Visual Studio 2003, GCC 3.3, Sun Studio and IBM XL through 2023 compilers, and Install.txt only asks for C++03 with RTTI and exceptions. In-core code exists for x86, x64, x32, ARM-32, Aarch64 and POWER8.
Streaming transformations where the Source/Filter/Sink pipeline is convenient, e.g. encrypt-and-encode or hash-while-copying with little glue code.

x86-64 servers with AES-NI and CLMUL, where AES and GCM dispatch to hardware code. Run the built-in `cryptest.exe b` benchmark (bench2.cpp covers AES/GCM with 2K and 64K tables, AES/CTR and CAST-128/CTR) against your current library before switching for speed.
when_not_to_use: As a throughput upgrade over OpenSSL for AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 or SHA-2. No current evidence shows Crypto++ ahead, and the only cross-library claim catalogued here is a 2013 CAST-128 result against libgcrypt.

Apple Silicon with the 8.9.0 release. Issue #1373 found that HasAES/HasSHA2/PMULL/NEON returned false on every Apple chip except a plain 'Apple M1', so the hardware paths were never selected. On an M1 Max the fix took AES-CBC from 252 to 866 MB/s and SHA-256 from 318 to 2071 MB/s.

Projects that need timely security releases. 8.9.0 (2023-10-01) is still the latest release, and fixes since then exist only on master: ChaCha SIMD carry, Ed25519 S >= L, OAEP underflow, DEFLATE HLIT. Release request #1345 has no maintainer reply, and issues #1247 (Marvin attack), #1249 (ModularSquareRoot DoS) and #1364/#1369 (zero-length AEAD tags accepted) are open.
FIPS 140 requirements. The Readme says the validated DLL moved to the CMVP historical list and should no longer be used.
New designs that would use CAST-128. Crypto++ itself files CAST-128 under 'insecure or obsolescent algorithms retained for backwards compatibility'.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (GNUmakefile builds libcryptopp.a / libcryptopp.so; MSVC solution for Windows). CMake and Autotools builds are unofficial side projects. vcpkg port available.
integration.min_toolchain: C++03 with 64-bit words, RTTI and exceptions; GNU Make 3.81+. The 8.9 Readme lists GCC 3.3-13.1, Clang 2.9-14, Apple Clang 4.3-12, VS2003-2022, Intel 9-16, Sun Studio 12u1-12.7 and IBM XL 10-14.
integration.platforms: x86, x86-64, x32, ARM-32/Aarch32, Aarch64, POWER8, with runtime CPU feature detection; portable C++ fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe at the class level (Readme): separate objects can be used concurrently, but you must synchronize when several threads use one Crypto++ object.

gotchas: Harness flaws behind the catalogued numbers (ketotek/crypto-bench). No library's output is checked. Crypto++ uses its own 0x01 key and 0x73 plaintext, while Botan and libgcrypt read the base-class key and in arrays, which are never initialized (CryptoppTest declares a shadowing key member). Crypto++'s encrypt_round builds std::string from the uninitialized out buffer with a strlen-style constructor, which is undefined behaviour and only works because fresh heap memory is zero. The AF_ALG row passes an 8-byte key (12-round reduced CAST5) and keys once. The libgcrypt baseline is stale: libgcrypt 1.6.0 (2013-12-16) 'improved performance of most cipher algorithms' and 1.9.0 (2021-01-19) made CAST5 '40% to 70% faster', enough to cover the 1.34x gap if that speedup applies to this CBC path (derived from page data). The counter-evidence is also flawed: scc-tw/cryptobench-cpp puts Crypto++ 8.9.0 at a flat 42-78 MB/s at 16 KiB for every algorithm on a MacBook Air, including portable BLAKE2b (78.2 vs Botan 1337.3) and SHA3-256 (74.4 vs Botan 601.4), which points to a build or dispatch problem (see issue #1373) rather than a fair comparison.

Zero-length authentication tags are accepted (issue #1364, open, PR #1365 unmerged): AuthenticatedDecryptionFilter with truncatedDigestSize 0 for GCM and ChaCha20Poly1305 DecryptAndVerify with macSize 0 report modified ciphertext as valid. Enforce a minimum tag length yourself.

The 8.9.0 release has two SIMD bugs that are fixed only on master. ChaCha on SSE2, NEON and Altivec (AVX2 was correct) gave a silent 1-bit keystream error when the 64-bit feed-forward add carried from word 12 into word 13 (issue #1362, fixed 2026-07-13). Apple chips other than a plain 'Apple M1' never selected hardware AES/SHA/PMULL (issue #1373, fixed 2026-10-01).

Pipeline ownership: an object passed by pointer (new StreamTransformationFilter(..., new StringSink(s))) is owned and deleted by the receiver, while objects passed by reference stay caller-owned. Builds that do not use the GNUmakefile must define NDEBUG and keep cryptlib.cpp, cpu.cpp and integer.cpp first in the build and link order (Readme).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Crypto++ over Botan or Mbed TLS only when you need its unusually wide or legacy algorithm catalogue, a C++03-era toolchain, or the pipeline API. For AEAD speed, the catalogued siblings (Botan's GCM vs OpenSSL at small sizes, libaegis or HiAE if you can change the cipher) have stronger and newer evidence than this 2013 CAST-128 result.
verified_claims_summary: ketotek/crypto-bench, a May 2013 third-party hobby harness, CBC-encrypts and decrypts a 4096-byte buffer 50000 times per library, re-creating the cipher and key schedule every round. It was built with g++ -O2 -march=corei7-avx against system libraries of unstated versions (Botan 1.10) on an unstated CPU. Its sample output, which is CPU time from clock() in MiB/s, has Crypto++ CAST-128 at 101.73/109.73 against libgcrypt CAST5 at 75.70/76.00 (about 1.34x/1.44x, derived from page data) and Botan CAST_128, run as a bare ECB block loop, at 96.69/97.17. The Linux AF_ALG row (135.10/315.98) is not comparable: it keys once outside the loop and passes an 8-byte key to setsockopt, so it runs the 12-round reduced CAST5 that RFC 2144 specifies for keys of 80 bits or less, against 16 rounds for the three libraries.
status_note: Master is active (last commit 2026-10-02) and the code is copyable (BSL-1.0 compilation, public-domain files), but the last release is still 8.9.0 (2023-10-01), cryptopp.com's certificates expired in April 2026 (#1347), and the cryptopp-modern fork (BSL-1.0, release 2026.9.1) is the packaged route to post-8.9.0 fixes and CVE patches (CVE-2023-50980, CVE-2023-50981, CVE-2024-28285). The catalogued speedup rests on a flawed 2013 CAST-128 harness against a since-accelerated libgcrypt (see gotchas), so treat it as historical.
